demographics: Very common in the general adult population; most adults report at least one episode in their lifetime
Slightly more common in women in clinic-based series
More frequent in people with high-stress lifestyles or irregular eating patterns

risk_factors.text: Eating large, high-fat or spicy meals
Eating quickly or at irregular times

family_history: Dyspepsia or peptic ulcer disease in a first-degree relative
social_history: Frequent dining out or late-night eating
exposures: Certain antibiotics, iron or potassium supplements

chief_complaints.text: My stomach feels upset after I eat
I get a burning or uncomfortable feeling in my upper belly
I feel bloated and keep belching
I feel full really quickly when I eat

hpi.onset: Gradual, often over days to weeks, and typically related to eating patterns or stress
hpi.duration: Recurrent episodes lasting minutes to a few hours; by definition often present for weeks to months when medical care is sought
hpi.progression: Comes and goes, usually worse after meals and better between meals; does not steadily worsen
hpi.location: Upper abdomen, around or just below the breastbone
hpi.radiation: May spread upward into the chest or throat; does not radiate to the back or right shoulder
hpi.quality: Burning, gnawing, or a sense of fullness and discomfort
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; usually 3–5/10, rarely severe
hpi.timing: Often within 30–60 minutes after eating; can also occur on an empty stomach
pertinent_negatives: Pain that wakes them from sleep
Pain radiating to the back or right shoulder
Chest pressure or pain with exertion

argues_against: Chronic cough or wheeze suggesting reflux-related airway disease
Symptoms driven primarily by an eating disorder

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with vague upper abdominal discomfort, early satiety or anorexia rather than classic burning; alarm features such as weight loss or anemia are more concerning for malignancy or ulcer.
Heartburn and indigestion are very common in the second and third trimesters due to hormonal and mechanical changes; symptoms are often worse when lying down.
missing_classic_features: Relation to dietary indiscretion or stress

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children cannot localize the discomfort and present with irritability, poor feeding, recurrent abdominal pain or vomiting.
missing_classic_features: Clear description of burning or meal-related pattern

atypical.how_it_differs: Autonomic neuropathy can cause delayed gastric emptying, so bloating, early satiety and nausea may dominate over burning.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort, may grimace or shift position during the visit
general.severe: Ill-appearing, diaphoretic, guarding the upper abdomen
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, lethargic, with signs of hypoperfusion

findings.finding: Mild to moderate epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding

findings.maneuver: Assess for rebound tenderness and involuntary guarding
findings.finding: No rebound tenderness or involuntary guarding

findings.finding: No pain with jarring or percussion

imaging.preferred_when: Right upper quadrant pain, jaundice or suspected biliary disease

initial.why: Looks for anemia or infection that would suggest ulcer bleeding or another cause
Noninvasive test for H. pylori, a common treatable cause of dyspepsia
Alternative noninvasive test for H. pylori
initial.only_if: stool antigen testing is unavailable or the patient prefers a breath test

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before imaging or medication selection
Direct visualization and biopsy when alarm features or high risk are present
initial.only_if: alarm features (weight loss, dysphagia, bleeding, anemia, age over 60 with new onset) are present

supporting.why: Rules out acute pancreatitis when pain radiates to the back or is severe
supporting.only_if: epigastric pain radiates to the back or is severe

supporting.why: Evaluates for gallstones or biliary disease
supporting.only_if: right upper quadrant pain, jaundice or suspected biliary colic

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.why: Evaluates for pancreatitis, perforation or mass when symptoms are severe or atypical
supporting.only_if: severe pain, suspected pancreatitis, perforation or mass

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management in uncomplicated dyspepsia
Not routine unless cardiac ischemia is suspected
Not routine in typical dyspepsia without biliary symptoms
not_indicated.only_if: right upper quadrant pain, jaundice or suspected biliary colic

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.only_if: severe pain, suspected pancreatitis, perforation or mass

decision_points: Test for H. pylori in all patients with dyspepsia who are not already known to be infected
Endoscopy for alarm features, age over 60 with new dyspepsia, or failure of empiric therapy
Pregnancy test before imaging or medication selection in anyone who could be pregnant
Consider cardiac ischemia if chest pain or risk factors are present

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Burning upper abdominal and retrosternal discomfort after meals is the classic overlap between dyspepsia and reflux

history: Heartburn and acid regurgitation are the dominant symptoms
Worse when lying down or bending over
Relieved by antacids or acid suppression
Water brash or sour taste in the mouth
imaging: Esophagitis or hiatal hernia on endoscopy
Normal endoscopy in non-erosive reflux disease

differential.name: Peptic ulcer disease
differential.why_considered: Epigastric burning pain is shared with dyspepsia, and ulcer is a common treatable cause
differential.trigger: NSAID use, H. pylori risk, or alarm features such as anemia, melena or night pain

history: Chronic NSAID or aspirin use
Nocturnal or fasting pain that may improve with food (duodenal) or worsen with food (gastric)
Melena or coffee-ground emesis
Family history of ulcer disease
labs: Positive H. pylori stool antigen or urea breath test
imaging: Gastric or duodenal ulcer on endoscopy
Free air on abdominal x-ray or CT if perforated

differential.name: Acute pancreatitis
differential.why_considered: Severe epigastric pain with nausea and vomiting can be mistaken for bad indigestion
differential.trigger: Severe constant epigastric pain radiating to the back, often with vomiting and a history of gallstones or heavy alcohol use

history: Severe, constant pain radiating to the back
Relieved by leaning forward
Heavy alcohol use or known gallstones
Vomiting that does not relieve the pain
labs: Lipase elevated more than three times the upper limit of normal
Elevated liver enzymes if biliary cause
imaging: Pancreatic enlargement or peripancreatic fluid on CT

differential.name: Acute coronary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Epigastric or upper abdominal discomfort can be the presenting symptom of myocardial ischemia, especially in older adults and people with diabetes
differential.trigger: Exertional or pressure-like upper abdominal or chest discomfort, diaphoresis, dyspnea, or cardiac risk factors

history: Pressure-like discomfort brought on by exertion and relieved by rest
Radiation to the left arm, jaw or shoulder
Diaphoresis, nausea, shortness of breath
Known coronary disease or multiple risk factors
exam: New murmur or signs of heart failure
imaging: Regional wall motion abnormality on echocardiography
ecg: T-wave inversion in a coronary distribution

differential.name: Biliary colic or cholecystitis
differential.why_considered: Right upper quadrant and epigastric pain after fatty meals overlaps with meal-related dyspepsia

history: Pain after fatty meals, lasting hours
Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain radiating to the right shoulder or back
Nausea and vomiting
Fever if cholecystitis
labs: Elevated alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin or transaminases
imaging: Gallstones or gallbladder wall thickening on ultrasound
Pericholecystic fluid or a distended gallbladder

differential.name: Gastric cancer
differential.why_considered: Early gastric cancer can present with vague dyspepsia before alarm features appear
differential.trigger: New dyspepsia in an older adult, unintentional weight loss, early satiety, anemia, or a family history of gastric cancer

history: Unintentional weight loss
Early satiety or anorexia
Progressive rather than intermittent symptoms
Dysphagia or vomiting if proximal or obstructing
imaging: Gastric mass, ulceration or wall thickening on endoscopy

differential.name: Functional dyspepsia
differential.why_considered: Persistent dyspepsia without an identifiable structural cause is common and is a diagnosis of exclusion

history: Symptoms for at least three months with onset at least six months earlier
No relief with defecation and no change in stool frequency or form
Postprandial fullness or early satiety
Normal evaluation including endoscopy
labs: Normal complete blood count and metabolic panel

severity.mild: Occasional episodes of upper abdominal discomfort or burning after large or rich meals, lasting minutes to a couple of hours, relieved by antacids or belching, with no interference in daily activities
severity.moderate: Frequent episodes over weeks, with bloating, early satiety and nausea, some avoidance of foods or activities, and mild epigastric tenderness on exam but no alarm features
severity.severe: Persistent or recurrent symptoms despite lifestyle changes and empiric acid suppression, with significant impact on eating, sleep or work, and possible weight loss or anemia that requires endoscopy
severity.critical: Not applicable; uncomplicated indigestion is not life-threatening, but severe pain, bleeding, or signs of perforation or cardiac ischemia require urgent evaluation

red_flags.meaning: Suggests an esophageal stricture, severe esophagitis or malignancy; needs endoscopy
Upper gastrointestinal bleeding, often from an ulcer or erosion; needs urgent evaluation
Raises concern for malignancy or a chronic inflammatory or malabsorptive process
Suggests obstruction, pancreatitis or another serious cause

red_flags.finding: Pain radiating to the back or right shoulder
red_flags.meaning: Suggests pancreatitis or biliary disease rather than simple dyspepsia

red_flags.finding: Chest pressure or pain with exertion, or shortness of breath
red_flags.meaning: Possible myocardial ischemia; needs immediate cardiac evaluation

red_flags.finding: Fever with severe abdominal pain or peritoneal signs
red_flags.meaning: Suggests perforation, cholecystitis or another acute abdomen
Suggests biliary obstruction or hepatobiliary disease

red_flags.finding: New dyspepsia in an older adult
red_flags.meaning: Higher risk of malignancy or ulcer; lower threshold for endoscopy

complications.name: Peptic ulcer with bleeding
clues: Epigastric pain that changes in character

complications.name: Chronic functional symptoms and reduced quality of life
clues: Avoidance of foods and social eating

special_populations.differences: May present with vague discomfort, early satiety or anorexia rather than classic burning; alarm features such as weight loss or anemia are more concerning for malignancy or ulcer, so endoscopy is recommended at a lower threshold.

Heartburn and indigestion are very common in the second and third trimesters due to hormonal and mechanical changes; symptoms are often worse when lying down, and medication choices must be pregnancy-safe.
Young children cannot localize the discomfort and present with irritability, poor feeding, recurrent abdominal pain or vomiting; the differential includes more congenital and infectious causes.
Autonomic neuropathy can cause delayed gastric emptying, so bloating, early satiety and nausea may dominate over burning; gastroparesis should be considered.
Increased intra-abdominal pressure and dietary patterns can worsen reflux and dyspepsia; weight loss is a useful part of management.

key_questions.question: Where exactly do you feel the discomfort, and can you point to it?
key_questions.looking_for: Upper abdomen, around or just below the breastbone

key_questions.question: When did this start, and how long has it been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over days to weeks; recurrent episodes over weeks to months when care is sought

key_questions.question: Does it come and go, or is it getting steadily worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Comes and goes, worse after meals and better between meals; steady worsening suggests another cause

key_questions.question: What does it feel like — burning, gnawing, or more of a fullness?
key_questions.looking_for: Burning, gnawing, or a sense of fullness and discomfort

key_questions.question: Is it related to eating? How soon after a meal does it start?
key_questions.looking_for: Often within 30–60 minutes after eating; can also occur on an empty stomach

key_questions.question: What makes it worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Large or high-fat meals, spicy foods, eating quickly, alcohol, caffeine, stress, lying down after eating, NSAIDs

key_questions.question: What makes it better?
key_questions.looking_for: Smaller more frequent meals, antacids, belching, sitting upright, relaxation

key_questions.question: Do you belch, feel bloated, or feel full very quickly when you eat?
key_questions.looking_for: Belching, bloating, upper abdominal fullness, early satiety

key_questions.question: Do you have heartburn or sour fluid coming up into your throat?
key_questions.looking_for: Heartburn or acid regurgitation; if dominant, points toward GERD

key_questions.question: Have you had any nausea or vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea sometimes; persistent vomiting is a red flag

key_questions.question: Have you had any trouble swallowing, or pain when you swallow?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; dysphagia or odynophagia suggests stricture, severe esophagitis or malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you vomited blood or coffee-ground material, or had black or tarry stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; hematemesis or melena indicates upper GI bleeding

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; unintentional weight loss raises concern for malignancy or chronic disease

key_questions.question: Does the pain ever wake you from sleep, or radiate to your back or right shoulder?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; night pain suggests ulcer, and back or shoulder radiation suggests pancreatitis or biliary disease

key_questions.question: Do you have chest pressure or pain with exertion, or shortness of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present symptoms suggest myocardial ischemia and need immediate cardiac evaluation

key_questions.question: Do you take NSAIDs, aspirin, steroids, or iron or potassium supplements?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAID, aspirin or steroid use raises the risk of ulcer; iron and potassium can irritate the stomach

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or drink alcohol, and how much?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking and heavy alcohol use both cause or worsen dyspepsia

key_questions.question: How would you describe your stress level and your eating pattern?
key_questions.looking_for: Ongoing stress, irregular meals, skipping meals, late-night or large high-fat meals

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had indigestion, an ulcer, or stomach cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of dyspepsia, peptic ulcer disease or gastric cancer

key_questions.question: Have you had an ulcer, reflux, H. pylori infection, or stomach surgery before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior peptic ulcer disease, GERD, H. pylori infection or gastric surgery

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes medication choices and the differential; test before imaging or medication selection

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or yellowing of the eyes or skin?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; fever with severe pain suggests an acute abdomen, and jaundice suggests biliary obstruction

reasoning_points: Upper abdominal burning or discomfort that comes and goes, typically within 30–60 minutes after eating
Relation to large, high-fat or spicy meals, eating quickly, alcohol, caffeine, stress or NSAIDs
Relief with smaller meals, antacids, belching or sitting upright
Associated belching, bloating, early satiety and sometimes nausea or heartburn
No alarm features: no dysphagia, odynophagia, hematemesis, melena, unintentional weight loss or persistent vomiting
Mild to moderate epigastric tenderness on exam without rebound, guarding or peritoneal signs
Normal or near-normal vital signs and no jaundice, pallor or organomegaly
Pregnancy excluded when relevant before imaging or medication selection
H. pylori testing considered, since it is a common treatable cause of dyspepsia
Endoscopy reserved for alarm features, new dyspepsia in an older adult, or failure of empiric therapy
Cardiac ischemia considered when chest pressure, exertional symptoms or cardiac risk factors are present

easy: Young or middle-aged adult with classic meal-related burning and belching
Clear relation to large, high-fat or spicy meals and stress
Mild epigastric tenderness with a benign abdominal exam
No alarm features and normal vital signs
medium: Overlap with GERD: heartburn and acid regurgitation are prominent
NSAID or aspirin use raising concern for peptic ulcer disease
Woman of reproductive age needing a pregnancy test before imaging or medication choices
Older adult with new dyspepsia requiring a lower threshold for endoscopy
Symptoms that persist despite lifestyle changes and empiric acid suppression
hard: Older adult with vague discomfort, early satiety or anorexia rather than classic burning
Diabetic patient with bloating, early satiety and nausea suggesting gastroparesis
Pregnant patient with heartburn and indigestion in the second or third trimester
Young child with irritability, poor feeding or recurrent abdominal pain who cannot localize the discomfort
Epigastric discomfort that is actually myocardial ischemia, especially with exertional symptoms or cardiac risk factors
Severe constant epigastric pain radiating to the back that turns out to be acute pancreatitis
